Common Recipes: Complete Examples from Printing to HTTP

This page gives, for each of the seven most common tasks, a piece of code you can compare against directly: the Sla spelling and the SA assembly spelling appear in pairs, all taken from demo / test files in the repository with their source paths noted. A recipe for which no real call site can be found is marked explicitly, and only the call form based on the contract signature is given.

hello world and println Formatting

The Sla spelling, from demos/rosetta/01_hello_world/main.sla:

@import "sa_std/io/print.sai"
@import "sa_std/fmt.sai"
@import "sa_std/string.sa"

fn main() -> i32 {
    println("hello, saasm");
    return 0;
};

Placeholder formatting, from demos/rosetta/05_struct/main.sla (04_loop/main.sla also has a multi-argument version, println("[{},{},{},{}]", zeroed[0], ...)):

let point = create_point(10, 20);
println("({},{})", point.x, point.y);

The SA assembly spelling — the compiler-generated main.sa in the same directory shows the true form of println("{}", result) (from demos/rosetta/02_mutability/main.sa):

tmp_4 = call @sa_fmt_u64(result, 10)
tmp_5 = call @sa_fmt_buffer_data(tmp_4)
tmp_6 = call @sa_fmt_buffer_len(tmp_4)
tmp_7 = tmp_5
call @sa_print_bytes(&tmp_7, tmp_6)
call @sa_fmt_buffer_free(^tmp_4)
@const SLA_STR_0 = utf8:"\n"
call @sa_print_bytes(&SLA_STR_0, 1)

When writing assembly by hand, the minimal form is a single call @sa_print_bytes(&msg, len); see the call @sa_print_bytes(&HELLO_MSG, 13) in sci/tests/llvm2sa_expected_hello.sa.

Reading a File into a String

Sla spelling A: through a project-side wrapper macro. The wrapper macro definition is from tests/import_fixtures/pkgjson/fs_helpers.sa:

@import "sa_std/fs.sa"

[MACRO] SLA_FS_READ_TO_STRING %out_buffer, %path, %path_len, %max_bytes
    __sla_fs_read_status_%out_buffer = 0
    EXPAND FS_READ_TO_STRING __sla_fs_read_status_%out_buffer, %out_buffer, %path, %path_len, %max_bytes
    !__sla_fs_read_status_%out_buffer
[END_MACRO]

The call site is from tests/test_unit_imported_fs_read_direct.sla:

@import "sa_std/string.sa"
@import "sa_std/fs.sa"
@import "import_fixtures/pkgjson/fs_helpers.sa"

fn imported_fs_read_missing(path_ptr: ptr, path_len: int) -> int {
    let buf = SLA_FS_READ_TO_STRING(path_ptr, path_len, 16);
    let len = SLA_FS_BUFFER_LEN(buf);
    return len;
}

Sla spelling B: calling the extern contract directly (a fallible handle; returning 0 indicates failure), from tests/test_unit_fallible_extern_payload_direct.sla:

@import "sa_std/fs.sai"

fn fallible_extern_read_len(path_ptr: ptr, path_len: u64) -> u64 {
    let buffer = sa_fs_read_file(path_ptr, path_len, 4096);
    switch buffer {
        0 => {
            return 0;
        },
        default => {},
    };
    let data_len = sa_fs_read_buffer_len(buffer);
    let free_status = sa_fs_read_buffer_free(buffer);
    if free_status != 0 {
        return 0;
    };
    return data_len;
}

Both contract signatures coexist in sci/sa_std/fs.sai: sa_std_fs_read_to_string(&path: ptr, path_len: u64, max_bytes: u64, &out_handle: ptr) -> i32 (status + out-parameter slot; macros use this one) and sa_fs_read_to_string(&path: ptr, path_len: u64, max_bytes: u64) -> u64! (a fallible handle; direct Sla calls use this one). For the macro list, see the fs chapter.

Reading Environment Variables / Command-Line Arguments

The contract core (from sci/sa_std/env.sai):

@extern sa_env_get(key: ptr, key_len: u64) -> u64
@extern sa_env_has(key: ptr, key_len: u64) -> i32
@extern sa_env_args_json() -> u64

The SA assembly spelling (a real test), from sci/tests/unit_framework/std_env_macro_surface.sa, whose top is @import "sa_std/env.sa":

@test "sa_std env args JSON macro"():
L_ARGS_ENTRY:
    EXPAND ENV_ARGS_JSON args_buffer
    EXPAND ENV_BUFFER_DATA args_ptr, args_buffer
    EXPAND ENV_BUFFER_LEN args_len, args_buffer

    args_buffer_nonzero = ne args_buffer, 0
    args_ptr_nonzero = ne args_ptr, 0
    args_len_nonzero = ne args_len, 0
    args_shape_ready = and args_buffer_nonzero, args_ptr_nonzero
    args_ready = and args_shape_ready, args_len_nonzero

    br args_ready -> L_ARGS_CHECK_JSON, L_ARGS_FAIL_READY

L_ARGS_CHECK_JSON:
    json_shape_ok = ne args_len, 0
    EXPAND ENV_BUFFER_FREE args_free_status, args_buffer
    EXPAND ENV_STATUS_IS_OK args_free_ok, args_free_status
NoteThere is no example in the repository of a .sla file calling the env contract. The Sla call form based on the signatures above is: let args = sa_env_args_json(); followed in order by taking sa_env_buffer_len(args) and sa_env_buffer_data(args), and finally sa_env_buffer_free(args); the same applies to sa_env_get(key, key_len). What is returned is a JSON array text buffer, which you must parse yourself (see the JSON recipe below).

Running a Child Process and Capturing Output

The contract core (from sci/sa_std/process.sai; note the prefix is sa_std_process_*):

@extern sa_std_process_run(&argv: ptr, argv_len: u64, &out_handle: ptr) -> i32
@extern sa_std_process_exec_capture(&argv: ptr, argv_len: u64, &out_code: ptr, &out_stdout: ptr, &out_stderr: ptr) -> i32
@extern sa_std_process_close(handle: u64) -> i32

The SA assembly spelling (a real test), from sci/tests/unit_framework/std_process_macro_surface.sa, whose top is @import "sa_std/process.sa". argv is an array of SaProcessArgv records, filled item by item with macros:

    argv = stack_alloc TRUE_ARGV2_SIZE
    output = stack_alloc ProcessOutput_SIZE
    argv0 = stack_alloc Slice_SIZE
    store argv0+Slice_ptr, &TRUE_BIN as ptr
    store argv0+Slice_len, TRUE_BIN_LEN as u64
    EXPAND PROCESS_ARGV_SET_SLICE argv, 0, argv0
    EXPAND PROCESS_ARGV_SET_CONST argv, 1, TRUE_ARG, TRUE_ARG_LEN

    EXPAND PROCESS_EXEC_CAPTURE_OUTPUT capture_status, output, argv, 2
    EXPAND PROCESS_STATUS_IS_OK capture_ok, capture_status

L_CAPTURE_OK:
    EXPAND PROCESS_OUTPUT_STATUS_PTR output_status_ptr, output
    EXPAND PROCESS_EXIT_STATUS_CODE output_code, output_status_ptr
    EXPAND PROCESS_OUTPUT_STDOUT_BUFFER stdout_buffer, output
    EXPAND PROCESS_OUTPUT_STDOUT_DATA stdout_ptr, output
    EXPAND PROCESS_OUTPUT_STDOUT_LEN stdout_len, output
    EXPAND PROCESS_OUTPUT_FREE free_status, output

On the Sla side there is a real example of importing this contract itself — let pid = sa_std_process_id(); in tests/test_unit_std_import.sla; but there is as yet no .sla call example for run / exec_capture in the repository, and their Sla call form needs to be wrapped by hand following the out-parameter pointer signatures above. See the process chapter for details.

TCP Connection or HTTP/2 Request

The contract has two surfaces: the complete sa_std_net_* and the simplified fallible surface sa_net_* (from sci/sa_std/net.sai):

@extern sa_net_tcp_connect(&host: ptr, host_len: u64, port: u32) -> u64!
@extern sa_net_tcp_listener_bind(&host: ptr, host_len: u64, port: u16) -> u64!
@extern sa_net_tcp_listener_accept(listener: u64) -> u64!
@extern sa_net_tcp_stream_write_all(stream: u64, &buf: ptr, len: u64) -> i32!
@extern sa_net_tcp_stream_read_exact(stream: u64, &buf: ptr, len: u64) -> i32!
@extern sa_net_tcp_stream_close(stream: u64) -> i32!

The SA assembly spelling (a real loopback test, excerpted, with status checks and jumps omitted), from the @support_net_surface() in sci/tests/unit_framework/support/stdlib_surface.sa. Here a fallible return appears as two slots, a “status word + handle”, with +0 the status and +8 the handle in this example:

L_ENTRY:
    listener_res = call @sa_net_tcp_listener_bind(&NET_LOOPBACK, NET_LOOPBACK_LEN, 0)
    listener_status = load listener_res+0 as u32
    listener = load listener_res+8 as u64
    ...
L_ADDR:
    addr_res = call @sa_net_tcp_listener_local_addr(listener)
    ...
    port = call @sa_net_addr_port(addr)
    host_copy = alloc host_len
    ...
L_CONNECT:
    connect_res = call @sa_net_tcp_connect(&host_copy, host_len, port)
    connect_status = load connect_res+0 as u32
    client = load connect_res+8 as u64
    ...
L_ACCEPT:
    accept_res = call @sa_net_tcp_listener_accept(listener)
    accept_status = load accept_res+0 as u32
    server = load accept_res+8 as u64

There is no example in the repository of a .sla file calling the net contract. For HTTP/2, likewise, there is as yet no call example in the repository; there are only the contract and the macro implementation; the call form, following the signature in sci/sa_std/http2.sai, is sa_std_http2_client_request(&url: ptr, url_len: u64, &method: ptr, method_len: u64, &body: ptr, body_len: u64, &out_handle: ptr) -> i32, and the corresponding macro on the SA side is the [MACRO] HTTP2_CLIENT_REQUEST %out_status, %out_buffer, %url, %url_len, %method, %method_len, %body, %body_len in sci/sa_std/http2.sa, with the result buffer taken out using the HTTP2_BUFFER_DATA / HTTP2_BUFFER_LEN / HTTP2_BUFFER_FREE trio. For the options and error surface, see the net chapter.

Parsing JSON and Fetching Values

Sla spelling A: calling the contract functions directly. From tests/test_unit_fallible_extern_payload_direct.sla:

@import "sa_std/fs.sai"
@import "sa_std/encoding/json.sai"
@import "sa_std/ptr.sa"
@import "sa_std/string.sa"

fn fallible_extern_json_free_status(node: ptr, owned: bool) -> i32 {
    if owned {
        return sa_json_free(node);
    };
    return 0;
}

@test "fallible consuming ptr extern closes a handle once"() {
    let root = sa_json_parse(STR_PTR("[{}]"), STR_LEN("[{}]") as u64);
    if PTR_IS_NONNULL(root) == false {
        panic(43013);
    };
    var child: ptr;
    child = PTR_NULL();
    let child_status = sa_json_array_get(root, 0, &child);
    if child_status != 0 || PTR_IS_NONNULL(child) == false {
        panic(43014);
    };
    let status = fallible_extern_json_free_status(child, true);
    if status != 0 {
        panic(43015);
    };
}

Sla spelling B: through the JSON macros. From tests/test_unit_imported_json_direct.sla:

@import "sa_std/string.sa"
@import "sa_std/encoding/json.sa"
@import "import_fixtures/pkgjson/json_helpers.sa"

fn imported_json_get_type(data: ptr, data_len: int) -> int {
    let root = JSON_PARSE(data, data_len);
    if JSON_KIND(root) < 0 {
        return -1;
    };
    let t = SLA_JSON_OBJECT_GET(root, STR_PTR("types"), STR_LEN("types"));
    return JSON_KIND(t);
}

@test "imported json direct sab"() {
    let got = imported_json_get_type("{\"types\":\"x\"}", 13);
    if got != 5 { panic(39022); };
}

Here SLA_JSON_OBJECT_GET is a project-side wrapper macro; in essence it wraps the out-parameter slot and then calls sa_json_object_get(node, &key, key_len, &out_handle); see tests/import_fixtures/pkgjson/json_helpers.sa. Fetching a scalar by key can take the shorter sa_json_object_get_i64 / _get_f64 / _get_string / _get_bool. For the complete contract, see the encoding chapter.

Assertion Testing

The full contract text (sci/sa_std/testing/assert.sai, four externs in total):

@extern sa_assert_eq_i64(actual: i64, expected: i64, code: i32) -> void
@extern sa_assert_eq_i64_at(actual: i64, expected: i64, code: i32, &file: ptr, file_len: u64, line: u32, col: u32) -> void
@extern sa_test_debug_i64(&name: ptr, name_len: u64, value: i64) -> void
@extern sa_test_fallible_i32_value(value: i32) -> i32!

The SA assembly spelling (a real test), from sci/tests/unit_framework/std_fs_macro_surface.sa, whose top is @import "sa_std/testing/assert.sai"; a failing branch first records the on-site scalars with sa_test_debug_i64, then closes with assertions:

L_FAIL_READ:
    call @sa_test_debug_i64(&FS_DBG_WRITE_STATUS, FS_DBG_WRITE_STATUS_LEN, write_file_status)
    call @sa_assert_eq_i64(write_file_status, SA_FS_OK, 940)
    call @sa_assert_eq_i64(exists_after_write, 1, 940)
    call @sa_assert_eq_i64(read_len, FS_TEST_HELLO_LEN, 940)
    call @sa_assert_eq_i64(read_eq, 1, 940)

For usage of the version with source location, see sci/docs/unit_test_framework.md: call @sa_assert_eq_i64_at(raw_status, 1, 103, *THIS_FILE, 14, 8, 5); the runner parses it into a panic location; on failure the output is PANIC[code]: expected=<expected> actual=<actual>.

The Sla spelling — a test body writes @test plus a conditional panic directly, from demos/rosetta/01_hello_world/main.sla:

@test "rosetta 001 01_hello_world"() {
    if str_eq("hello, saasm", "hello, saasm") != true {
        panic(1);
    };
};
Notesa test isolates each @test in a separate process, so a single assertion failure does not interrupt the remaining tests; assertion details can be cross-checked against the testing chapter and the API Index.

Three Commandments for Hot-Path Scratch Space (2026-11-02)

1. Do not declare a large stack array per call on a hot path. Each declaration of [0u8; N] re-fills the full size byte by byte (measured at ≈4 ns/byte, unrelated to the actual amount written): a per-call scratch array of 8192 bytes ≈ +33 µs/op. 4096 is the verified safe side; for larger scratch space, use a persistent field (zero-filled once at construction) or heap allocation.
2. Do not create a new Vec per call. The cost of creating a Vec once is more than allocation: the deep drop at the end of the scope walks the elements one by one and, in measurements, accounts for a considerable share of service time. Append in bulk using the geometric-growth primitives (@sa_vec_reserve_grow / @sa_vec_extend, 0→4 doubling); do not use incremental growth with exact reservation.
3. Persistent buffer + mark/rewind. A hot path holds one persistent Vec: before filling, take a mark with sa_vec_mark, and after processing, sa_vec_rewind to truncate back (deep elements are each properly dropped; the byte surface uses the sa_vec_rewind_bytes fast path). Capacity is retained and allocation goes to zero. Evidence (slaredis, first cut): the persistent scratch + rewind form brought c1 SET service time down from 76.6 µs to 40.9 µs.
